content.overview: A low final yield is an outcome, not a diagnosis. Loss-stage analysis asks where units failed or waited, what they shared and which next observation can separate competing explanations.

vocabulary.definition: A stage or resource whose effective capacity limits the output of the larger process.
The defined process interval in which a unit first failed to meet continuation criteria.

sections.title: Localize before explaining
sections.body: Separate intake rejection, early wilt, rooting failure, contamination, acclimation loss and release hold. Each pattern points to a different evidence set.

sections.title: Shared factors rank hypotheses
sections.body: Donor, genotype, media lot, tray zone, operator period, equipment and environment can create structured patterns. Association narrows the next check but does not prove cause.

sections.title: Delay can be the controlling failure
sections.body: Material may survive but miss a production window because a stage is variable or review is slow. Track both biological loss and time in state.

workedExamples: A normal rooting rate with long release holds points toward review or evidence flow rather than root initiation.
Loss concentrated after acclimation should not be corrected only by changing cutting intake.
commonMistakes: Using final yield as a root cause.
Ignoring units delayed in hold status.
content.practicalApplication: Build a stage-loss waterfall and time-in-state chart for four mock batches, identify the limiting stage and propose the next measurement that best separates the top two hypotheses.
content.summary: Bottleneck analysis locates loss and delay before assigning cause, then uses shared-factor evidence to choose the next discriminating check.
